title: Habitual qat chewing and short-term response to conservative management of temporomandibular disorders: A prospective cohort study in conflict-affected Yemen
content:
by Raji Mansoor Hajeb, Yousif Osman Yousif, Nader Ahmed Al-Aizari, Essam Ahmed Al-Moraissi

Qat (Catha edulis), chewed daily by a substantial proportion of Yemeni adults, contains cathinone, an amphetamine-like alkaloid that augments masticatory muscle activity. Observational evidence links the habit to temporomandibular disorders (TMD), yet none has examined how chewers respond once treated. A prospective cohort of 148 consecutive patients diagnosed by Research Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders Axis I examination was followed at Sana’a University and Al-Kuwait Teaching Hospital between October 2018 and October 2020. Fifty-four (36.5%) were habitual qat chewers, defined as three or more sessions weekly. All received reassurance, education and self-care advice, to which the clinician added an NSAID, diazepam, amitriptyline or a stabilization splint as routine care. The outcome was a patient-reported global rating of change at three months, dichotomized as improved or not improved; every patient attended that visit. Improvement occurred in 47 of 54 chewers (87.0%) and 88 of 94 non-chewers (93.6%), a difference of 6.6 percentage points (95% CI −16.8 to 3.7; Fisher exact p = 0.23). The crude odds ratio for improvement among chewers was 0.47 (95% CI 0.15–1.42); it reached 0.92 (95% CI 0.26–3.29) once age and sex were entered, chewers being older and age the only consistent predictor of non-improvement. Treatment components did not differ between groups. Pain presented differently in chewers rather than simply more severely: 29.6% reported none and 24.1% severe pain, none falling in the mild band, so the bands differed in shape (p < 0.001) but not in rank (p = 0.22). Among those in pain, 38 of 40 chewers rated it moderate or severe against 52 of 82 non-chewers. Conservative management benefited nine patients in ten. Powered only for a difference of 16 percentage points or more, the study cannot exclude a clinically meaningful disadvantage to chewers; all adjusted estimates rest on 13 events and are hypothesis-generating.
